rationales.A: Carnegie sits on the money while workers stand outside, so he did not share it.
rationales.B: The cartoon shows Carnegie in charge, whip in hand, above his own mill.
rationales.C: Carnegie reclines on money bags with a whip while crowds of workers stand outside a closed mill: rich above, workers shut out below.
rationales.D: The cartoon shows Carnegie keeping the mill and the money, not selling it.
rationales.general:
Put the two halves of the picture together.
1. On top, Carnegie reclines on piles of money bags, whip in hand.
2. Below, crowds of workers stand outside a mill marked closed and lock-out.
3. Rich above and shut-out workers below is a contrast, not a partnership.
4. So the point is that Carnegie grew rich while his workers went without.
Remember: a cartoon’s top and bottom often argue against each other.

stimulus.text: Political cartoon “Promise and Performance,” published in 1892. A large Andrew Carnegie sits on piles of money bags, holding a whip. Below him stretches a steel mill with signs reading “CLOSED—STRIKE,” “CLOSED,” and “LOCK-OUT.” Crowds of workers stand outside the mill gates.
